newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal union hails success of worker action.
newsitem.headline: German metal union hails success of worker action.

text.p: IG Metall, Germany's most powerful trade union, said on Thursday the surprise pay deal reached overnight in the state of Lower Saxony showed the power of mass protests by workers against planned cuts to sick pay entitlements.

The metal and engineering union, whose near three million members makes it the largest trade union in the world, has been at the forefront of protests involving hundreds of thousands of workers against a new law cutting sick pay.
IG Metall deputy chairman Walter Riester said that, faced with the prospect of further damaging stoppages, engineering firms had put pressure on industry negotiators to come to an agreement.
"Companies are suffering because of the delay in coming to an agreement and they are not prepared to accept that any more," Riester said on German Radio.

In an unexpected move, regional employers in the northern state of Lower Saxony agreed earlier to continue paying workers sick pay at 100 percent of salary, overriding a new law allowing them to cut payments to 80 percent.
Under the deal, 90,000 workers in Lower Saxony will also receive a wage increase of 1.5 percent from April, 1997 and a further rise of 2.5 percent from April 1, 1998.
In return for full sick pay, end-of-year bonuses will fall by five percent to 55 percent of salary.
Riester warned the Gesamtmetall metal and engineering employers federation not to veto this deal as the union believes it did to a recent pact in the steel-making region of North Rhine-Westphalia.
"If Gesamtmetall now tries blocking tactics on sick pay in other regions, it's not going to get any cheaper (for the companies involved)," he said.

Gesamtmetall president Werner Stumpfe has previously denied that he overruled any agreement in North Rhine-Westphalia, where talks broke down last week, saying that regional employer negotiators themselves broke off talks.

All-out strikes in the metal and engineering sector, which includes German industrial giants from steel-maker Thyssen AG to car maker Mercedes, were expected to start next spring if the dispute continued.
But union officials said on Thursday they were now hopeful that other regions would now agree deals that kept full sick pay intact.
Gesamtmetall, which had been hoping the new law would provide it with the start of what it says is a much-needed reduction in German labour costs, was less enthusiastic about the deal.

Estimating, however, that the overall deal would leave costs for an average firm in the sector almost unchanged, it said regional employer groups would decide on whether to adopt the model for a deal in the coming weeks.
